title: Rule 'homicide,' lawyers urge
article: Lawyer Patrick Ducharme pushed for a homicide verdict at the Robert Carpenter inquest Wednesday, arguing Amherstburg police officers exacerbated the situation when they used themselves as "battering rams" to gain entry to Carpenter's home without cause.

Andrew Bradie, lawyer for the officers involved in Carpenter's shooting death, countered that police acted with courage, made split- second decisions based on their training and "did what they had to do" to ensure the safety of a fellow officer and Carpenter's two young children.
Coroner's counsel Robert Ash also pushed for a homicide verdict, but stressed such a verdict implies no culpability and simply meant the killing of one by another.

Ash argued the officers "had no choice" but to enter Carpenter's home at 258 McCurdy Dr., given the charged circumstances they encountered Oct. 30 when they responded to a disrupted 911 call shortly after 7 a.m.

Although there has been conflicting testimony during the 12-day inquest, the jury was told that Carpenter's common-law wife, Lisa Stewart, made a whispered 911 call shortly before 7 a.m. and hung up before her address was confirmed. Attempts to obtain it were thwarted by deficiencies in Bell Canada's 911 system.
Carpenter's address wasn't in the 911 database because he had been given a new phone number on a Saturday. Calls made to Bell's 24- hour hotline were twice forwarded to a pager.
Ash, who was "shocked" and "stunned" to learn of the "glaring" deficiencies in Bell's system, asked the jury to send a "very strong message" to Bell that the situation is "unacceptable."
The jury heard evidence that Carpenter was paranoid in the days before his death, but his mother and a woman who spoke to him just prior to the shooting tell a different story.

Ash said Carpenter was a "walking time bomb" buckling under stresses including chronic pain, relationship troubles and financial woes. He referred to a 1984 incident in which Carpenter was hospitalized and the testimony of a neighbour who said Carpenter believed he was being poisoned less than 24 hours before his death.
"What happened that day didn't just arise out of the blue," said Ash. "There was an awful lot going on here before police knocked on that door."

Ducharme argued police didn't try to calm Carpenter when they arrived at his house and that Carpenter was justified in requesting a search warrant. He said "raw emotion" compelled the officers to ram Carpenter's door because he allegedly assaulted a police officer.

Bradie countered that the incident would never have happened if Carpenter had answered the door in a "civilized manner." He said the officers had to act because children were crying inside the house and Stewart told them Carpenter was armed.
